title: Sell Mineral Rights in Garfield County, CO
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Garfield County, CO | Piceance Gas
metaDescription: Own Piceance Basin gas minerals in Garfield County? We price interests from Rifle to Parachute off real decline data and close directly with owners.
heroLead: Garfield County is the historical center of Piceance Basin gas development in Colorado, and mineral ownership here spans everything from decades-old vertical wells still paying modest royalties to large undeveloped tracts that have never been leased.
intro: Piceance gas is fundamentally a different asset than the oil-driven DJ Basin production owners farther east are more used to hearing about. Wells in the Mamm Creek, Rulison, and Grand Valley fields around Rifle, Silt, New Castle, and Parachute produce primarily from the Mancos and Williams Fork formations, and development pace here has always tracked natural gas prices closely rather than following a steady, predictable schedule.

That gas-price sensitivity created real boom-and-slowdown cycles across the county: dense vertical and directional drilling through the mid-2000s, a long pullback as gas prices sat depressed for years, and periodic renewed permitting activity since, concentrated in areas where operators already hold established infrastructure. If your family has held Garfield County minerals for a while, there is a good chance the interest has seen at least one productive period, even if things look quiet right now.

We buy Garfield County mineral interests directly, whether they are currently producing, held by older production that has gone dormant, or entirely unleased ranch and agricultural ground. Pricing depends heavily on which of those three categories your tract falls into, and we walk through that with you before quoting anything.

sections.heading: Mamm Creek, Rulison, and the eastern county fields
paragraphs: The dense drilling that built much of Garfield County's Piceance production history happened east of Glenwood Springs, around Silt and Rifle, where operators developed the Mamm Creek and Rulison fields with hundreds of wells through the 2000s boom. Interests in this area typically have long, well-documented production histories, which we price using a decline curve fit to your actual check stub data rather than a generic assumption for the basin.

Because so much has been drilled and sold in this corridor, we also have deep comparable sale data to check any decline-curve-based offer against, giving owners here more pricing confidence than in less-developed parts of the county.

sections.heading: The western county and Grand Valley gas fields
paragraphs: Farther west toward Parachute and the Grand Valley, similar Mancos and Williams Fork gas development has occurred, though with its own distinct permitting and infrastructure history separate from the Rifle-Silt corridor. We evaluate western county interests on their own production record rather than assuming they mirror the eastern fields.

sections.heading: Undeveloped ranch and agricultural acreage
paragraphs: A meaningful share of Garfield County mineral ownership sits under ranch and farmland that has never been leased, or was leased during a past regional push without any well following. We price this speculative acreage against comparable regional lease and sale activity, and we are direct that these offers run lower than producing-interest offers, since there is no revenue stream to underwrite against.

Split estate is common throughout the county, meaning the surface owner and mineral owner are often different people. That does not change your right to lease or sell your mineral interest, but it does affect how quickly an operator can negotiate the surface access needed to actually drill, which we factor into how we time-adjust value on undeveloped acreage.

sections.heading: Title work through Garfield County records
paragraphs: We pull recorded leases, division orders, and unit agreements from the Garfield County Clerk and Recorder to confirm your exact net revenue interest. This step matters more here than in a newer basin, because Piceance assets have changed operators multiple times over the past two decades as larger companies sold mature holdings to smaller ones, and we want your paperwork to match current reality before finalizing an offer.

faqs.question: Why has drilling activity in Garfield County slowed down at various points?
faqs.answer: Piceance wells are primarily gas plays, and gas prices have been softer than oil prices for extended stretches over the past decade, which slows new permitting even when existing wells keep producing.

faqs.question: Is an older, declined well in Garfield County still worth selling?
faqs.answer: Often yes. We price the remaining production off your actual check stub trend using a decline curve, rather than assuming peak output has continued.

faqs.question: My royalty operator has changed names multiple times over the years. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: No, this is common across the Piceance Basin as assets have changed hands between operators. We confirm the current operator of record before finalizing any offer.

faqs.question: How is undeveloped Garfield County acreage priced differently than producing acreage?
faqs.answer: Producing acreage is priced off a decline curve applied to real revenue. Undeveloped acreage is priced against comparable regional lease and sale activity, since there is no production history to underwrite against, and typically prices lower.

faqs.question: Does split estate ownership complicate a sale?
faqs.answer: No, you can sell your mineral interest regardless of who owns the surface. Split estate mainly affects how quickly a future operator can negotiate surface access for new drilling, which we factor into how we value undeveloped acreage.

faqs.question: What documents speed up a Garfield County offer the most?
faqs.answer: A division order and several months of recent check stubs for producing interests. For undeveloped acreage, a copy of your deed and any historical lease paperwork, even if expired, helps us price accurately.
